It does not constitute hiring criteria, an ability score, or an evaluation of job competence, nor does it constitute any food hygiene, safety, legal, or investment advice. This page corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 35-9031.00 occupation "Hosts and Hostesses, Restaurant, Lounge, and Coffee Shop" (hosts and hostesses): welcoming patrons, seating them at tables or in the lounge, and helping ensure the quality of facilities and service. Official scope text: Welcome patrons, seat them at tables or in lounge, and help ensure quality of facilities and service. The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET (the precise occupation 35-9031.00 scope); the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; the two jurisdictions and their employment systems must not be applied to one another.

To judge whether hosting suits you, first run one verifiable greeting drill using public or simulated materials: set up a fictional dining scenario (for example, a dinner rush with a mix of reservations and walk-ins), and write a step-by-step process from greeting and welcoming, verifying reservations and asking about needs, checking table availability, seating by party size and needs, delivering menus and handing over to servers, to wait list management and records, marking the check points at each step and the possible abnormalities (full house and overbooking, special dietary or accessibility needs, unhappy waiting customers, children or large parties, hygiene and facility problems). Afterward, check: whether hygiene and safety requirements (clean tables, facility checks, clear walkways) are treated as non-omittable items; whether requests that cannot be met are written as a polite explanation with alternatives; and whether facility or service problems are written up as reportable issues. Test with a real deliverable, not just answers to an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | The work activities for U.S. O*NET 35-9031.00 show that performing for or working directly with the public, getting information, assisting and caring for others, and communicating with others are the most important activities for this occupation; work context shows a high proportion of constant contact with others, positions dealing with external customers or the public generally require long-term direct contact with customers, face-to-face discussions and telephone communication are frequent, and the workplace is an indoor dining environment with considerable walking and standing. The most important skills include active listening, speaking, service orientation, and coordination. If you are willing to stand and walk for long periods during peak hours, face all kinds of customers directly, and patiently handle waiting and requests, these daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (35-9031.00): the work centers on direct customer contact, managing the wait list, and coordinating seating, and involves dealing with unhappy or agitated customers, keeping order during peak hours, and considerable standing and walking. This occupation deals with customers, tables, and facilities: a single seating mistake, a single ignored special need, or a single unreported facility or hygiene problem can affect the customer experience and the establishment's reputation. This page therefore lists hygiene and facility checks, wait list and reservation management, and identifying special needs and service handover separately. On the U.S. side, this occupation is marked Bright Outlook, and the O*NET summary shows a projected decline (-2%) from 2024 to 2034, with about 107,700 job openings per year and employment of about 429,900 in 2024; growth is negative but the openings mainly come from replacement needs. If it is hard for you to sustain intense standing during peak hours, long periods of direct customer interaction, or emotional pressure, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Commitment judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things within the same shift at once: make the hosting solid (verifying reservations and needs, seating by table and service capacity, handing over to servers and maintaining wait list order, producing reviewable seating and wait list records); keep hygiene and facilities under control (checking table and facility cleanliness, keeping walkways clear, reporting abnormalities, acting per institutional and hygiene requirements); and carry definable position responsibility (be responsible for the accuracy of your own reception and coordination, and report matters beyond your authority such as facility issues or complaints under institutional rules). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a step-by-step greeting process and seating record, or a drill on recognizing and handling common arrival situations), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of hosts and hostesses can be broken down along three lines: (1) greeting and seating—welcoming customers, verifying reservations and needs, and checking tables and seating parties; (2) waiting and service handover—managing the wait list and order, explaining wait times, delivering menus, and handing over to servers; (3) facilities and records—checking table and environmental cleanliness, reporting facility problems, and maintaining seating and wait list records. The three lines share the same set of hygiene and coordination requirements, but their deliverables go to different recipients: greeting and seating serve the customer experience, handover serves the service team, and records serve the operations ledger.

O*NET 35-9031.00 "Hosts and Hostesses, Restaurant, Lounge, and Coffee Shop": welcoming patrons, seating them at tables or in the lounge, and helping ensure the quality of facilities and service. Core tasks are greeting and welcoming patrons, verifying reservations and needs, checking tables and seating parties, delivering menus and handing over to servers, managing waiting and the wait list, and keeping facilities clean and reporting problems. Job Zone Levels One to Two (little to some preparation needed).

entries.answer: Waiters and waitresses focus on taking orders, serving food, and tableside service; food counter attendants focus on counter sales and food preparation; cashiers focus on payment and settlement; concierges serve hotel and mixed-use venue guests; and food service managers handle scheduling and operating decisions. subject.summary: Hosts and Hostesses, Restaurant, Lounge, and Coffee Shop corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 35-9031.00 occupation "Hosts and Hostesses, Restaurant, Lounge, and Coffee Shop": welcoming patrons, seating them at tables or in the lounge, and helping ensure the quality of facilities and service. Official scope text: Welcome patrons, seat them at tables or in lounge, and help ensure quality of facilities and service. Core tasks include greeting and welcoming patrons, verifying reservations and needs, checking tables and seating parties, delivering menus and handing over to servers, managing and recording the wait list, and checking tables and the environment and reporting problems. The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET (the precise occupation 35-9031.00 scope); the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; China's employment and food hygiene institutional boundaries are labeled separately.
